---
title: "Writing with AI, but for humans"
subtitle: "About 75 minutes, plus an optional stretch"
---

::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** A chatbot is a good interviewer, critic, and proofreader.
  But your writing is for people: the reader, who needs it to be right and
  specific, and you, who will answer for every sentence. So get the ideas
  clear first, use the tool for the help the piece's rules allow, and say
  exactly how you used it.
- **What you do.** Follow one worked example in ChatGPT Edu, step by step: a
  setup block in one chat, a feedback skill, an interview, your own draft,
  a feedback-and-edit loop, a final edit, a reader check, and a disclosure. Then
  do the same with a piece of your own.
- **What you keep.** A finished piece with every version saved, a setup
  block you can reuse, the feedback skill, and a disclosure that says what
  AI did at each step.
- **Short on time?** Read "11:40 p.m., the last experience entry", then do
  Steps 1 to 6 of the Do with your own piece (45 minutes).
- **Want more?** The optional stretch runs the whole workflow on a vaguer
  problem, with research, an AI draft, and reviews, and, if you like, a skill
  you build yourself (about two hours).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Set up one ChatGPT Edu chat for a piece of writing, with your rules and
   your rubric.
2. Add a skill to your account and use it in a loop: feedback, an edit (by
   you or by the AI), re-upload, until your rubric is met.
3. Keep every version, check the last one with a reader, and write a
   disclosure that says exactly what AI did.
4. Explain why the goal is writing that is right for its reader and for you,
   not writing that hides AI use; what residency applications and medical
   journals ask for; and why a detector score is not proof that someone
   cheated.

Course competencies: AIM-4 (ethics, law, and regulation), AIM-5 (clinical
use), AIM-X (professional identity).
:::

**What you need.** Your university **ChatGPT Edu** account, on a laptop. One
real piece of writing you need in the next month that is not about a patient,
or none: the worked example works on its own. A blank document for your
versions. This chapter goes with week 2's Wednesday talk on professional
writing and the optional hands-on session that afternoon. About 15 minutes of
reading and about 70 of doing. Doing it again with your own piece is a second
session.

::: {.callout-note title="On Copilot or a personal ChatGPT account?"}
The screens below are ChatGPT Edu at CU Anschutz, checked on 21 October 2026.
Other accounts may not have **Skills**. Without them, paste the text of the
feedback skill (Step 3) into your setup block. Everything else works the same
in any chat.
:::

## 11:40 p.m., the last experience entry

It is late, and you are finishing the last experience entry on your residency
application. The experience is two years of Saturday mornings at a student-run
free clinic. You ran the supply room. You know exactly what happened there,
but every version you type sounds dull. So you paste your notes into a
chatbot and ask it to write the entry.

::: {.chat-pair}
<div class="chat-pane">
<div class="prompt">Turn my notes into a residency application experience entry, about 120 words. Notes: free clinic, 2 yrs, Saturday mornings. ran the supply room. glucose test strips ran out twice in January, people went home without a sugar check. made a paper log with a minimum count for each item, taught the first-years to use it. hasn't run out since. boring job but I liked it. what I learned: a lot of problems that look like people problems are really system problems.</div>
<div class="reply">
<p>Serving as Supply Coordinator at a student-run free clinic was a pivotal experience that underscored the critical importance of systems-level thinking in delivering equitable care. When I identified recurring shortages of glucose test strips, I spearheaded the development of a comprehensive inventory management system and fostered a culture of accountability among my peers. This initiative not only ensured seamless continuity of care, but also deepened my lifelong commitment to serving underserved communities. Ultimately, this experience showcased my leadership abilities and my passion for improving health systems.</p>
</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative. Notes and reply written for this chapter; not a transcript of any real tool or real applicant.</div>
</div>
:::

It reads well. It is the right length. But your best details are gone: the
paper log, the first-years, "it hasn't run out since". Your one honest line,
"boring job but I liked it", is gone. In their place are words you never use,
like "pivotal" and "spearheaded". And one sentence says something you never
said: a "lifelong commitment to serving underserved communities".

In three weeks an interviewer will read this entry aloud and say, "Tell me
about that." Which version do you want to be answering for? The Do below
writes the other version, step by step, and you can follow along.

## Why this matters

You will write for the rest of your career: emails to attendings, abstracts,
fellowship applications, letters for students. A chatbot can help with all of
it. It is quick at finding what is unclear, what is missing, and what is too
long.

Whether anyone can tell is not the point. In three blinded studies, faculty
who read personal statements could not reliably tell which were written by
ChatGPT (@fig-readers). In the largest, readers for medical school
admissions gave the AI-written essays slightly *higher* scores than the
human-written ones, 5.02 against 4.67 on a 7-point scale [@pmid:41051105].
That does not make an AI-written statement allowed; the rules are below.

::: {#fig-readers}
<div class="acc-bars" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart of how often readers correctly said whether a personal statement was written by a person or by ChatGPT. Orthopaedic surgery residency, 8 readers: 52 percent. Medical school admissions, 17 readers: 56 percent. Pediatrics residency, 4 readers: 59 percent. A dashed line at 50 percent marks a coin toss.">
<div class="acc-row"><span class="lbl">Orthopaedic surgery residency, 8 readers</span><span class="track"><span class="bar" style="width:52%"></span><span class="val" style="left:52%">52%</span></span></div>
<div class="acc-row"><span class="lbl">Medical school admissions, 17 readers</span><span class="track"><span class="bar" style="width:56%"></span><span class="val" style="left:56%">56%</span></span></div>
<div class="acc-row"><span class="lbl">Pediatrics residency, 4 readers</span><span class="track"><span class="bar" style="width:59%"></span><span class="val" style="left:59%">59%</span></span></div>
<div class="acc-row axis"><span class="lbl"></span><span class="track"><span style="left:0%">0%</span><span style="left:50%">50%</span><span style="left:100%">100%</span></span></div>
</div>

How often faculty readers correctly said whether a statement was written by a
person or by ChatGPT. The dashed line at 50 percent is what a coin toss would
score. Redrawn for this chapter from the papers' numbers:
orthopaedics, 41 of 79 guesses, the sum of the paper's two counts
[@pmid:42005879]; medical school admissions [@pmid:41051105]; pediatrics
[@pmid:41584952]. The data are the papers'; the drawing is this course's.
:::

In a study of professional creative writers, 30 readers surveyed online
could not tell AI-assisted work from solo work either. They showed less
concern about co-writing with AI than the writers did
[@doi:10.1145/3711020]. This chapter is not about hiding AI use. It is about
the two people the writing is for.

- **Your reader needs it to be right and specific.** A generic piece tells a
  reader little. In 62,132 residency personal statements from one US center,
  a set of words linked to chatbots rose from 27.9 percent of statements
  before 2024 to 45.6 percent in 2024 [@pmid:42890249]. The details only you
  have are what the reader came for.
- **You will answer for it.** Copying a chatbot's text lowered people's sense
  that the writing was theirs; writing a draft first and then using the
  chatbot kept it close to writing alone [@doi:10.1038/s41598-026-42312-6].
  The professional writers in the study above described authenticity as
  coming more from how they wrote than from the finished text
  [@doi:10.1145/3711020]. And a chatbot draft can say things you do not
  believe, like the "lifelong commitment" above.

**Say exactly how you used it.** Medical journals require this. The ICMJE
asks authors to describe how they used AI, in the cover letter and in the
paper, and says that not disclosing it may be treated as misconduct
([ICMJE, "Use of AI by Authors"](https://www.icmje.org/recommendations/browse/artificial-intelligence/ai-use-by-authors.html),
checked 21 October 2026). One proposed format, GAIDeT, lists the specific
tasks handed to AI and the person who checked them, instead of "we used
ChatGPT" [@pmid:40781729]. Being open has a cost. In 13 experiments, people
who disclosed AI use were trusted less. Being exposed by someone else cost
more [@doi:10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104405]. In a study of 40 news readers,
detailed disclosures lowered trust, while one-line labels did not. Even so,
about two-thirds of the readers preferred the detailed version
[@doi:10.1145/3805689.3812386]. Be specific, and let your reader judge.

**Ideas first.** The course director gets the ideas clear first: what to
say, and what the reader should take away (@fig-workflow). After that, a
chatbot can do a lot. It can build a detailed outline, research the
background that frames it, and even write a first draft to rework. What
goes wrong is asking for a draft before the ideas are yours. Then the chatbot
supplies the ideas. You get its average piece, with views you may not hold. There is a trade-off even when
the ideas are yours: the more of the draft a chatbot writes, the less the
piece tends to feel like yours [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2604.11009]. You decide
how much help to take for each piece, and you say what you chose. Stuck at a
blank page? A rough first draft from your own notes can get you moving, as
long as the ideas in it are yours.

**Review from the reader's side.** Whoever drafted it, the test is the
reader. Did the ideas you meant come across, with the impact you wanted? A
personal statement's reader wants something warm and personal. An abstract's
reader wants something strong and factual. A patient letter's reader wants
something easy to follow. So the rubric below says what your reader wants,
and every review in the Do checks the draft against it, not against whether
it "sounds like AI".

![How the course director writes with AI, when the piece's rules allow it. The first row ends with clear ideas: an interview if there is a rubric, a rough plan if not, then research, summarizing, and refining until the ideas are clear. Only then does drafting start. Review from the reader's side sends the draft back to editing, and the last step is a section saying how AI was used. Drawn for this course.](../images/writing-workflow.svg){#fig-workflow fig-alt="Flowchart in two rows. Row one: a decision, rubric given? Yes leads to AI interviews you for the details; no leads to a rough scope in an AI chat. Both lead to research, then summarize and refine, then a checkpoint, the ideas are clear, which loops back to refine if not yet. Row two: draft, perhaps in sections; edit, you and AI on the same file; fine-tune display and format; AI review from the reader's side, which loops back to editing when it has feedback; write how AI was used. A legend colours each step by who leads: mostly you, together, or mostly AI."}

**The rules for the piece decide the rest.** The AAMC's guidance on the
residency personal statement says: "The use of AI tools is acceptable for
brainstorming, proofreading, or editing the personal statement, but the final
submission should represent your own work."
([AAMC, "Personal Statement"](https://students-residents.aamc.org/applying-residencies-eras/publication-chapters/personal-statement),
checked 18 October 2026, for the 2027 ERAS season.) So for an application,
write the draft yourself; that is why the worked example below does. The
ICMJE does not forbid AI help with drafting a paper; it asks you to say how
you used it and holds you responsible for the result. Conferences,
fellowships, and newsletters set their own rules; read theirs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="If you have more time: the evidence in detail"}
**Sameness.** **Voice** here means what makes a piece yours: the details you
noticed, the words you would choose, and the views you hold. A chatbot writes the most likely next words, so a chatbot personal
statement is close to the average personal statement.

- In the 62,132 statements above, 2024 statements also used about three fewer
  first-person words ("I", "my", "me") each [@pmid:42890249]. The study
  counted words; it did not prove who used a chatbot.
- When people wrote essays with a chatbot, essays by
  different writers became more alike. The sameness came from the text the
  model wrote; the text the writers wrote themselves stayed as varied as
  before [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2309.05196].
- Ideas from a chatbot made each writer's story score higher, but the stories
  written with AI ideas were more similar to each other [@pmid:38996021].
- Indian writers using AI suggestions shifted toward American ways of
  writing [@doi:10.1145/3706598.3713564]. If English is not your first
  language, the "polish" a chatbot adds may also remove what makes your
  writing yours.
- Reviewers described research abstracts they suspected were machine-written
  as "vaguer and more formulaic" [@pmid:37100871].

**Ownership.** **Ownership** here means the sense that a piece of writing is
yours: you made the choices in it, and you can explain each sentence. In an
experiment planned in advance and registered before any data were collected, copying a chatbot's text lowered ownership,
confidence, and how meaningful the work felt; drafting first and then using
the chatbot gave results close to writing alone
[@doi:10.1038/s41598-026-42312-6]. A second study found that help with
planning lowered ownership least and help with writing the draft lowered it
most, while more help made the essays better [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2604.11009].
That trade is real. You decide how much of it you want for each piece.

**Views you do not hold.** A writing assistant set up to favour one side of a
question moved what 1,506 people wrote, and their later survey answers
[@doi:10.1145/3544548.3581196]. A "why this specialty" paragraph is an
argument about yourself. Decide what you think before you ask the chatbot
anything.

**Detectors and "humanizers".** An **AI detector** scores how likely a text is
to be machine-written; a **humanizer** rewrites machine text so detectors miss
it. Seven detectors labelled 61.3 percent of human-written English-test
essays by non-native writers as AI-written [@pmid:37521038]. Statements that
two detectors flagged in one surgery program more often showed features of
writers whose first language is not English [@pmid:40537315]. Paraphrasing AI
text dropped one detector's success rate from 70.3 to 4.6 percent
[@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2303.13408]. So a detector score is not proof that
someone cheated. A humanizer's whole job is to hide AI use. This chapter aims
for the opposite: a piece that is right, and an honest account of how it was
made.
:::

## The method at a glance

Each step of the Do uses one part of ChatGPT Edu for one job. The parts are
listed here so you know where each thing lives.

| Step | Where in ChatGPT Edu | Its job |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Write your rubric | Your own document | Say what "done" means before you open the chatbot |
| 2. Set up one chat | **New chat**, **Medium** thinking, a pasted setup block | Hold everything about this one piece: the rules for the chatbot and your rubric |
| 3. Add the feedback skill | **Customize > Skills** | A way of working you reuse on any piece: feedback first, a rewrite only when you ask |
| 4. Interview | The same chat | Bring back the details only you know |
| 5. Write v0 | Your own Word file | The core, in your words |
| 6. The loop | The same chat, each version attached | Feedback, then an edit by you or by the AI, then re-upload, until done |
| 7. Final edit | Your own Word file | Your hands last; note what you changed |
| 8. Reader check | A real person who stands in for your reader, or the skill again | What actually came across, compared with your rubric; feedback goes back to editing |
| 9. Disclose | Your own document | Say exactly what AI did at each step, and what you did |

: Where each step lives. The setup block holds the piece, the skill holds the method, and the prompt holds today's request. {#tbl-method}

The rule in the caption answers a question students ask: where do
instructions go? Facts and rules about *this piece* go in the setup block. A
method you will use on *every piece* goes in a skill. What you want *right
now* goes in the prompt.

professor (KevinMD, 1 September 2026; 18 min; automatic captions on YouTube).
<https://kevinmd.com/2026/09/she-spent-weeks-on-her-personal-statement-then-someone-asked-why-she-didnt-use-ai-podcast.html>
Listen for her argument that the value of a personal statement is what you

## Do: one entry, start to finish

You will follow one worked example: the free clinic entry from the opening.
Every step shows what to click or paste, then what you should see. Do each
step twice if you can: once with the example, once with your own piece. If
you have no piece of your own today, the example alone is enough.

No patient information. If your piece mentions a patient, replace that
passage with `[patient story]` before you paste anything. The chatbot does not
need it to help you. [What counts as patient
information](../course/patient-information.qmd). Your CV and unpublished
results are not patient information, but they are yours: use ChatGPT Edu,
not a personal account.

Keep every version as its own file: `entry-v0.docx`, `entry-v2.docx`,
and so on, plus the feedback pasted into a notes file. You can
compare any two in Word with **Review > Compare**. If you ask ChatGPT to edit
a file, it gives you back a new file to download; save that as the next
version too.

### Step 1. Write your rubric (5 minutes)

Before you open ChatGPT, write down what "done" means. This is your
**rubric**: you will judge every version against it, not against how polished
it sounds. Copy this and fill it in:

```
What I am writing:   ____________________________________
Who reads it:        ____________________________________
What they want:      ____________________________________
  (warm and personal? strong and factual? easy to follow?)
The one thing they
should know about me: ____________________________________
If asked about it,
I would say:         ____________________________________
Done when:           ____________________________________
Rules:               ____________________________________
```

Here is the worked example, filled in:

```
What I am writing: the experience entry for my residency
  application (ERAS) about the student-run free clinic supply
  room. About 120 words.
Who reads it: residency program faculty reading many applications.
What they want: to meet a specific person, quickly; warm and
  concrete, not polished and general.
The one thing they should know about me: I notice when a problem
  is really a system problem, and I fix it in a way other people
  can keep using.
If asked about it, I would say: the glucose strips ran out twice,
  I made a paper log with a minimum count, taught the first-years,
  and it has not run out since. It was a boring job and I liked it.
Done when: it is in my words, in the first person, keeps the paper
  log and the first-years, and every sentence is something I can
  explain without looking.
Rules: AAMC: AI is acceptable for brainstorming, proofreading, or
  editing; the final submission should represent my own work.
```

The **Done when** line matters most. It is what tells you, and the chatbot,
when to stop.

### Step 2. Start one chat, and set it up (5 minutes)

Everything for this piece happens in **one chat**, so ChatGPT keeps your rules
and your rubric in view the whole time.

1. Go to [chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com). Check that the bottom left says
   **CU - Anschutz (Edu)**.
2. Click **New chat**. Next to the box where you type, it says **Instant** or
   **Medium**. Click it and move the **Thinking effort** slider to
   **Medium**. Instant is fast but less careful.
3. Paste this setup block, with your rubric from Step 1 at the bottom, and
   send it:

```
For this chat, I'm working on one piece of my writing. The ideas
and the details are mine. Help me by interviewing me, giving
feedback, checking spelling and grammar, and drafting or rewriting
when I ask, using only the ideas and details I have given you. Mark
anything you add with [ADDED]. Judge every version against my rubric
below. Answer in plain English, briefly. Reply "Ready" for now.

My rubric:
[paste your rubric from Step 1]
```

If you have a style you want kept, add a line for it, for example: `My
style: I use contractions and dashes. Keep them.` Students in this course
found a line like this kept their style in light edits.

You should see a short "Ready". The setup lets ChatGPT draft from your ideas
when you ask. For the worked example you write v0 yourself anyway, because
the AAMC wants the final residency statement to be your own work.

::: {.callout-tip title="Coming back to this piece later? Use a project"}
A chat can get long and start forgetting its early parts. If you will work on
a piece over several days, a **project** keeps the setup for you: in the left
sidebar, click the **+** next to **Projects**, choose **Project-only memory**
(so your other chats stay out), paste the setup block into **⋯ > Project
settings > Instructions**, and start each session with a new chat inside it.
For one sitting, a plain chat is simpler.
:::

### Step 3. Add the feedback skill (5 minutes)

A **skill** is a saved set of instructions for one kind of task. ChatGPT
reads each skill's short description and uses the skill by itself when your
request matches it. Unlike a setup block, a skill works in every chat
without pasting.

This course's skill gives feedback on a draft first. It rewrites only when you ask, and only from your ideas. It
reviews the draft against five points (Accurate, Aligned, Appropriate, Tone,
Unbiased), the editing checklist from the week 2 writing talk, and against
your rubric. It quotes the words it means, lists common chatbot words, asks
you one question an interviewer might ask, and keeps its feedback unless you
give it a reason to change.

1. Download the skill:
   [writing-feedback SKILL.md](../downloads/writing-feedback/SKILL.md){download="SKILL.md"}.
   Open it and read it first. It is plain text, about one page.
2. In ChatGPT, click the **Plugins** icon in the narrow bar on the far left.
   The **Customize** page opens. Click **Skills**.
3. Click **Add**, then **Upload from your computer**.
4. Choose the `SKILL.md` file you downloaded. You should see *Skill
   uploaded*. Click **Done**.

You should see **writing feedback** under **Installed**.

::: {.callout-warning title="Read a skill before you upload it"}
ChatGPT warns that skills from other people "may try to access your data".
That warning is right. A skill is instructions that ChatGPT follows, so read
any skill before you add it, including this one. If a skill asks the model to
send your text somewhere, or to do something you did not ask for, do not use
it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="No Skills in your account, or want to make your own?"}
**No Skills?** Open `SKILL.md`, copy everything below the second `---` line,
and paste it into your chat after the setup block. It will work in that chat
only.

**Make your own.** On the **Skills** page, **Add** also offers **Create with
editor** (a name, a description of when to use it, and the instructions) and
**Create with chat**. In a chat, the **+** menu has **Template Creator**,
which turns a prompt you keep reusing into a skill. Skills can be much larger
than this one. For manuscripts and grants, see scriptorium in Go deeper.
:::

### Step 4. Let ChatGPT interview you (10 minutes)

In the same chat, paste this:

```
I'm writing the piece described in my rubric. Don't write
it yet. Interview me first: ask me one question at a time,
five in all, that help me remember specific details: what I saw,
what I did, what changed, and what I'd do differently. Wait for my
answer before the next question.
```

You should see one question, about the piece in your rubric, and nothing
else. When we ran this, the first question was:

::: {.chat-pair}
<div class="chat-pane">
<div class="reply">
<p><strong>Question 1 of 5: What you saw</strong></p>
<p>Think back to when the glucose strips ran out at the student-run free clinic. What did you actually see or hear that first made you realize there was a problem? Describe the specific moment as you remember it.</p>
</div>
<div class="fine">From a test run in ChatGPT Edu on 21 October 2026, with the worked example's rubric. Your questions will differ.</div>
</div>
:::

Notice that it found the free clinic in your rubric without being told. Answer in plain, quick sentences; typos are fine. Or click **Dictate**,
the microphone next to the box, and just talk. When a question brings
back a detail you had forgotten, copy it into your document.

### Step 5. Write v0 yourself (10 minutes)

Look away from the chat. In Word (or any document), write the core of
the piece: 100 to 250 words, in the first person, with at least two details
from the interview. Aim for true and specific, not polished.

The worked example's v0:

```
For two years I ran the supply room at our student-run free clinic
on Saturday mornings. In January we ran out of glucose test strips
twice, and both times a patient with diabetes went home without a
sugar check. It wasn't that people were careless; nobody knew how
many strips we had left. I made a paper log, taped it to the cabinet
with a minimum count for each item, and taught the first-years to
check it at the end of every shift. We haven't run out of anything
since. It was a boring job, and I liked it. It showed me my passion
for improving health systems for every patient.
```

It is good, and it is not done. Keep reading before you judge it.

### Step 6. The loop: feedback, edit, re-upload (15 to 20 minutes)

Save it as a file, for example `entry-v0.docx`. Back in the same chat, click
**+ > Add files** to attach it, and send it with one line:

```
Here is my first draft (v0), attached. Can you give me feedback on it?
```

You do not have to name the skill. Asking for feedback on your own draft is
what its description says, so ChatGPT uses it. You should see feedback under
five headings (their wording may vary), each quoting your words. Then come
the two least clear sentences, spelling and grammar fixes, and one interview
question. It should not offer a new version. If it rewrites your draft
instead, add: `Use the writing feedback skill.`

Here is part of what came back for the worked example (shortened):

::: {.chat-pair}
<div class="chat-pane">
<div class="reply">
<p><strong>1. Accuracy</strong><br>"We haven't run out of anything since." The Rubric only establishes that the glucose strips haven't run out again. Can you support the broader claim about <em>anything</em>?</p>
<p><strong>2. Alignment with the Rubric</strong><br>Weakest alignment: "It showed me my passion for improving health systems for every patient." The Rubric asks readers to recognize your practical approach to fixing systems. This sentence makes a broad claim rather than adding evidence of that approach.</p>
<p><strong>4. Tone</strong><br>[...] This sounds like a general application statement. "Passion" and "every patient" could appear in many applicants' essays. By contrast, "It was a boring job, and I liked it." is distinctive.</p>
<p><strong>One interview question.</strong> How did you decide what minimum count to put on the paper log, and what made that number useful?</p>
</div>
<div class="fine">Excerpt from a test run in ChatGPT Edu on 21 October 2026, Medium thinking, with the writing-feedback skill. Your feedback will differ.</div>
</div>
:::

Read this as a list of places to look, not a list of orders. Here it found
two real problems: the last sentence claims more than the story shows, and
"anything" is bigger than what you know. It also told you which line to
keep. Paste the feedback into your notes file as **v1 feedback**.

**Now edit, either way.**

- **Ask the AI to edit.** Name the points you agree with, and ask for the
  file back:

  ```
  Make these changes and give me back the edited .docx: fix
  "anything" to what I know, and cut the last sentence. Change
  nothing else. Mark anything you add with [ADDED].
  ```

  ChatGPT returns a new file to download (tested on 21 October 2026). Open it
  and check every change.
- **Or edit it yourself.** Open your file in Word and make the changes.

Save the result as the next version, for example `entry-v2.docx`.

**Then re-upload and ask again.** Attach the new file with **+ > Add files**:
`Here is v2, attached. Can you give me feedback on it?` Keep going round:
feedback, edit, re-upload. **Stop** when the feedback only questions things
you have chosen to keep, and your rubric's **Done when** line is met. Take the
points you agree with, and ignore the rest; you decide.

After one pass, the worked example's v2 kept the boring job, fixed
"anything", and answered the interview question instead of claiming passion:

```
For two years I ran the supply room at our student-run free clinic
on Saturday mornings. In January we ran out of glucose test strips
twice, and both times a patient with diabetes went home without a
sugar check. Nobody was careless; nobody knew how many strips we
had left. I made a paper log, taped it to the cabinet with a minimum
count for each item, set at two weeks of our busiest use, and taught
the first-years to check it at the end of every shift. The strips
have not run out since. It was a boring job, and I liked it.
```

### Step 7. Your own final edit (10 minutes)

**Your last version, in your hands.** Read it out loud. Change anything you would not
say. Then look for words that make writing read as generic, because they
turn up everywhere: *delve, underscore, showcase, pivotal, intricate, realm,
meticulous, foster, seamless, spearhead, passion, passionate, journey,
tapestry*. Keep a word only
if it is the word you mean. If there is a word or character limit, count it
yourself in your word processor. Chatbots often report that they hit a count
when they have not. Then reread the whole piece. If you change anything,
reread it again from the top. You are done when you read it all the way
through without making an edit. Save it as your final version.

In your notes file, write two lines:

```
What I changed from v0 to the final, and why: ____________________________
Where the chatbot helped / where I overruled it: _____________
```

Those two lines are the point of saving versions. They show you what the
tool is good for in your writing, and what it is not.

### Step 8. Read it as your reader would (10 minutes)

The test is what a reader takes away. A real person is the best check you
have.

**Ask one person.** Pick someone who could stand in for your reader: a
classmate, a resident, a friend who reads applications. Send them your final version with
one question:

```
In one sentence, what did you learn about me from this? Which
sentence would you ask me about?
```

No patient information goes to them either. If what they learned is not
the one thing in your rubric, that is the edit to make. If they would ask
about a sentence you cannot explain, fix that sentence.

**If no one is free,** attach your final version in the same chat and ask for
feedback again (Step 6). The skill starts with what came across. Compare
that with your rubric's "What they want" line.

**Feedback goes back to editing.** Edit it yourself for each point you agree
with.

**Last, your own check.** Read it aloud, one sentence at a time. Could you
explain each one to an interviewer without looking? Is it true? Would you
say it this way?

### Step 9. Say exactly how you used AI (5 minutes)

"AI was used" tells your reader nothing. Say which tool, what it did at which
step, and what you did. Your versions are the record, so this takes a few
minutes. The worked example's disclosure:

```
How I used AI: I wrote every sentence of this entry myself. I used
ChatGPT Edu to interview me before I wrote, to give feedback on my
first draft against my own rubric, and to check spelling. I chose
which feedback to use and made every change myself.
```

Where it goes depends on the piece. For a journal article, follow the
journal's rules; the ICMJE asks for it in the cover letter and in the paper.
For an application, include it where the application asks. If it does not
ask, keep it with your versions, ready for an interviewer who does. Anywhere
else, keep it with the piece, ready for anyone who asks. This book does the same:
its [AI ledger](../appendix/ai-ledger.qmd) records what AI did for each
chapter and who checked it.

### Now do it with your own piece

Go back to Step 1 with a piece you need: a thank-you email after an
interview, an abstract, a scholarship paragraph, or one of your own
experience entries. Start a new chat with its own setup block (Step 2). The skill is already
installed, so skip Step 3.

### When the rules allow an AI draft

For a paper, a newsletter piece, or a teaching handout, the rules may allow
a chatbot to write a first draft. This is the short version; the stretch
exercise below has the full one, with research. Keep Steps 1 to 4, replace Step 5, and keep
the rest.

1. **Your setup block already allows this.** It lets ChatGPT draft when you
   ask, from your ideas only.
2. **Get the ideas clear.** After the interview in Step 4, write, in your own
   words, the three to five points the piece must make. These are the ideas;
   they stay yours.
3. **Ask for an outline, then check it.**

   ```
   Here are the points this piece must make: [your points].
   Build a detailed outline for the piece in my rubric.
   Search for background that frames these points, with links.
   Do not add points I did not give you; list any you think are
   missing separately, with your reason.
   ```

   Open the links. Cut what is wrong. Add or drop points yourself.
4. **Ask for a first draft from your outline.**

   ```
   Write a first draft of the piece from the outline above. Use only
   my points and the sources I kept. Mark any sentence where you
   added a claim I did not give you.
   ```

   Save it as **v0 (AI draft)**.
5. **Carry on from Step 6.** The loop, then your own final edit. In Step 8,
   check hardest for sentences you would not say.
6. **Say so in Step 9.** For example: "ChatGPT Edu built the outline from my
   points, found background sources, which I checked, and wrote a first
   draft. I revised every paragraph."

### What you keep

- **Your finished piece**, with every version and your two lines on what you
  changed.
- **Your setup block** with your rubric, ready for the next draft.
- **The feedback skill**, in every chat from now on.
- **Your disclosure**, specific to this piece.
- **One sentence for question 2 of your [learning
  journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd):** where the chatbot helped, where
  you overruled it.

## Stretch (optional): a vague problem, the whole workflow

Most real writing starts vaguer than an application entry. Someone asks for
"a proposal" or "a handout", and you do not yet know what you think. This
exercise runs the whole workflow in @fig-workflow, including an AI draft.
Pieces like these often allow one, but ask whoever asked for the piece, and
put the answer on your rubric's Rules line. It is guided, not step by
step: each stage has a goal, a prompt to start from, and a check before you
move on. How you get there is up to you. Plan on about two hours, over more
than one sitting.

**Pick one problem.**

- **A proposal.** Your clerkship director asks for a one-page proposal:
  should students use ChatGPT Edu on rotations, and if so, how?
- **A teaching handout.** A one-page handout for third-year students
  starting a rotation, on something you know well: presenting a new
  admission, a good sign-out, or reading a chest film.

No patient information. Any example in your piece is made up.

**Set up.** Over two hours or more, a project helps: make one with
**Project-only memory** (the tip in Step 2) and paste this into its
**Instructions**. In one sitting, paste it at the top of a new chat instead.

```
This is one piece of my writing. I decide the ideas. You may
interview me, research, outline, and draft from my points when I
ask. Mark any claim I did not give you with [ADDED]. Judge every
version against my rubric. Answer in plain English, briefly.
```

### Stage 1. Scope it

**Goal:** a rubric you wrote yourself. Nobody gave you one, so you make it.

```
I've been asked for [the piece] by [who]. I don't know my position
yet. Don't write anything yet. Ask me up to seven questions, one at a
time, to scope it: who reads it, what they need to decide or do,
length and format, limits, and what success looks like.
```

**Check:** write the rubric yourself from your answers, using the template in
Step 1 of the Do. Change "about me" to "from this piece". Add it as the
**Rubric** source.

### Stage 2. Research

**Goal:** four to six sources you have opened and read.

```
Find [what you need: policies, guidance, evidence, teaching
resources] on [the topic], with links. For each: who wrote it, the
date, and one sentence on what it says. Mark anything you could not
open or check.
```

For a bigger question, **Deep research** is also in the **+** menu.

**Check:** open every link you plan to keep. Delete any source that does
not say what the chatbot said it says. Keep a list of the ones you keep, each
with a summary in your own words, and paste that list into the chat.

### Stage 3. Get the ideas clear

**Goal:** three to five points in your own words, each with an answer to
its strongest objection. This is the checkpoint in @fig-workflow.

```
Summarize where my sources agree and disagree, in eight bullets,
each with its source.
```

Then write your points yourself, and ask:

```
My points are: [your points]. What is the strongest objection to
each? Which of my points do my sources not support?
```

**Check:** close the chat. Can you state each point and answer its
objection without looking? If not, go back to research or change the
point. Do not draft yet.

### Stage 4. Draft, in sections

**Goal:** a first draft, v0, built from your points.

```
Draft [the first section] from my points and the sources I
pasted. Use only my points. Mark any claim I did not give you with
[ADDED].
```

Draft one section at a time, and read each one before asking for the next.
If your account has **Documents** in the **+** menu, you can try keeping the
draft there. Otherwise, keep it in your own document.

### Stage 5. Edit together

**Goal:** v1 and v2, where every sentence is one you would sign.

Edit it yourself first. Then ask for small, named changes: `Cut section 2 to
120 words without losing [point].` or `Make this paragraph plainer for a
third-year student.`

**Check:** no **[ADDED]** tag is left unresolved. The tag can be missed, so
read for claims yourself. Every claim traces to a source you opened or to
your own point.

### Stage 6. Polish the format

**Goal:** one page a busy reader can scan.

```
Suggest a one-page layout for this: headings, and a table if it
helps. Do not change my wording.
```

### Stage 7. Review, then back to editing

**Goal:** a version that holds up for its readers.

First run the feedback skill (Step 6 of the Do): `Here is my draft. Can you
give me feedback on it?` Then do the reader check (Step 8) with a real person:
for the proposal, someone who knows the clerkship; for the handout, a
third-year student.

**Check:** every point you agreed with goes back to Stage 5 and is edited
in. Stop when the reviews only question things you chose to keep.

### Stage 8. Say how AI was used

**Goal:** a short section at the end, stage by stage. For example:

> **How AI was used.** I scoped the proposal with ChatGPT Edu, which asked me
> questions; I wrote the rubric. It found sources; I opened each one and
> kept five. I wrote the three points and answered its objections. It
> drafted each section from my points; I edited every paragraph. It
> reviewed the draft, and a classmate read it; I made four changes.

### Optional: build your own skill

The feedback skill from Step 3 works on any piece. If you write one kind of
piece often, such as abstracts, a skill for that kind can hold its rules.

**Goal:** a feedback skill of your own for one kind of piece, which runs when
you ask for it.

1. Click the **Plugins** icon (Step 3), then **Skills > Add > Create with
   editor**. (In a chat, the **+** menu also has **Template Creator**.)
2. **Name:** for example `abstract-feedback`. **Description:** say when to use
   it, for example: `Use when I ask for feedback on a conference abstract I
   wrote. Feedback first; rewrite only when I ask, from my ideas.`
3. **Instructions:** start from the writing-feedback skill's text. Add the
   rules for this kind of piece: the word limit, the required sections, what
   reviewers score, and what the reader wants from it.
4. Click **Create**.

**Check:** in a new chat, ask for feedback on an abstract. Does your skill
run? If the general feedback skill answers instead, say `Use the
abstract-feedback skill.` Does it keep to your rules? Change the instructions
and try again. A skill you write is a set of instructions under your name,
so read it again before you share it with anyone.

### What you keep from the stretch

- **A one-page proposal or handout**, with every claim traced to a source you
  opened or to your own point.
- **A list of the sources you kept**, and why.
- **A section on how AI was used**, stage by stage.
- **Optional: your own feedback skill for one kind of piece.**

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| A set-up chat (objective 1) | Medium thinking and a setup block with your rules and your rubric | A chat with no rubric |
| Feedback on your own draft (objective 2) | A v0 you wrote, and feedback that quotes your words and does not rewrite them | A chatbot rewrite, lightly edited |
| The loop (objective 2) | At least two rounds of feedback, each followed by an edit you chose, with every version saved | One round, or edits you did not check |
| Versions and reader check (objective 3) | Every version saved; one reader's one-sentence takeaway compared with your rubric, and the edits it led to; each sentence read aloud | Only the final version, or no one read it |
| Stretch, if you did it | Points you can state, with their objections answered, without looking; every claim traced to a source you opened or to your own point; review feedback edited in; a stage-by-stage disclosure | A polished draft whose points you cannot defend |
| What changed, and the disclosure (objective 3) | Two lines on what you changed and why; a disclosure that names the tool and what it did at each step | "AI was used" |
| The reasons and the rules (objective 4) | One sentence on why the goal is a piece that is right for its reader and for you, not one that hides AI use; what the AAMC allows and what the ICMJE asks; why a detector score is not proof | "So no one can tell", or "AI is not allowed" |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close the chapter. Two specifics.

First, go back to 11:40 p.m. and the free clinic entry. Compare the chatbot's
entry with the worked example's v2. Then answer the interviewer who reads
your v2 aloud and says, "Tell me about that." You should be able to answer
without looking.

Second, name the next piece of writing you will do with a chatbot. Are the
ideas clear yet? What do its rules allow? Which steps will you keep: the
rubric, the setup block, the interview, writing v0 yourself or an AI draft from
your outline, the feedback loop, the checks, and the
disclosure?

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The three blinded studies in @fig-readers: orthopaedic surgery residency
  [@pmid:42005879], pediatrics residency [@pmid:41584952], and medical school
  admissions, where a detector named the author correctly 91 percent of the
  time. The authors still judged its false alarms too frequent to use it
  [@pmid:41051105].
- How much of the biomedical literature now shows chatbot vocabulary. At
  least 13.5 percent of 2024 PubMed abstracts did, and up to 40 percent in
  some groups of journals [@pmid:40601754].
- What authenticity means to professional writers who co-write with AI:
  their process and their sense of self, more than the text. Readers could
  not tell the AI-assisted work apart and showed less concern about it than
  the writers [@doi:10.1145/3711020].
- Saying how you used AI: the GAIDeT taxonomy for listing the tasks handed to
  AI [@pmid:40781729]; 13 experiments on the trust cost of disclosing, and
  the larger cost of being exposed [@doi:10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104405]; and
  news readers' preference for detailed disclosures
  [@doi:10.1145/3805689.3812386].
- How well a model copies your style from examples of your writing: partly,
  with a drift toward a general, average tone [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2509.14543].
- Brain activity and memory in people writing essays with and without a
  chatbot. People who wrote with a chatbot struggled to quote their own
  essays. This is a **preprint, not yet peer-reviewed**, with small groups,
  and its methods have been criticized; treat it as a question, not an answer
  [@doi:10.48550/arXiv.2506.08872].

**Tools**

- [scriptorium](https://seandavi.github.io/scriptorium/), a larger set of
  skills built on the same idea as this chapter's: critique of prose the
  author already wrote, with no scores and no drafting from a blank page by
  default. It is for manuscripts and grants (citation audit, reviewer
  simulation, argument flow, and others) and runs in Claude Code or Codex,
  not ChatGPT. Its [case study](https://seandavi.github.io/scriptorium/concepts/case-study/)
  shows real output. Written by the course director.

![One scriptorium skill, citation-audit, run on a made-up manuscript paragraph. Each row is one claim, the citation behind it, how well the citation supports it, and a recommendation. It adds no citations and changes no prose; the author decides. Screenshot of the [scriptorium case study](https://seandavi.github.io/scriptorium/concepts/case-study/), Sean Davis, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); cropped, with the site's menus hidden.](../images/scriptorium-citation-audit.png){#fig-scriptorium fig-alt="A table with five rows and the columns Claim, Citation, Strength, Assessment, and Recommendation. Example row: the claim 'Our findings extend the existing literature on bariatric-surgery outcomes' cites thompson2021, rated 'Weak fit', because the cited paper is a narrative review that does not address the pattern the paragraph claims to extend; the recommendation is to cite a primary cohort study or soften the framing."}
